nameStory: The 'Shaggy Mane' gets its name from the distinctive white, scaly cap that looks remarkably like a disheveled wig or a lion's shaggy mane. It's also called 'lawyer's wig' in some places, perhaps because those white scales resemble the powdered wigs once worn by attorneys and judges in British courts.
description: The Shaggy Mane is a distinctive white mushroom that starts life looking like a white cylinder poking up from the ground, then opens into a bell-shaped cap covered in fluffy white scales. These mushrooms are famous for their dramatic disappearing act - within hours of maturity, they turn black and literally dissolve themselves into an inky mess. When young and fresh, they're completely white with a clean, pleasant appearance, but they're very short-lived once they start opening up.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: White bell-shaped cap covered in distinctive shaggy white scales that feel soft and fluffy to the touch, like cotton or fur

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Gills start pure white, then turn pink, and finally black before the entire mushroom dissolves into black ink

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, hollow white stem that feels firm when young but becomes fragile as the mushroom ages

idTips.label: Dissolving Behavior
idTips.description: The entire mushroom turns black and melts into an inky liquid within hours - this dramatic self-destruction is unique and unmistakable

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a pleasant, mild mushroom smell with no unpleasant odors when young

habitat: Look for Shaggy Manes in disturbed areas like lawns, roadsides, gravel paths, parking lot edges, and waste ground throughout New England. They prefer rich, well-fertilized soil and often pop up in suburban areas after lawn treatments or soil disturbance. You'll rarely find them in deep woods - they love human-modified landscapes.

seasonality.spring: Early specimens may appear in late spring during warm, wet periods, especially in well-fertilized areas.
seasonality.summer: Common after summer rains, particularly in July and August when warm temperatures and moisture combine perfectly.
seasonality.fall: Peak season runs through September and October, with the largest flushes often appearing after autumn rains until hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent - these mushrooms cannot tolerate freezing temperatures and die back completely.

funFact: Shaggy Manes literally digest themselves to spread their spores - the black 'ink' they dissolve into is packed with millions of spores, and this auto-digestion process is so reliable that the ink was once used as writing ink and for making photographs!
confusionNotes: Young Shaggy Manes could be confused with some deadly Amanita species when they're still in their white cylindrical stage, but Amanitas have a bulbous base and never have the characteristic shaggy scales. Remember: if it doesn't have those fluffy white scales, it's not a Shaggy Mane.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'ink cap,' Shaggy Manes belong to a group of mushrooms that have been reclassified recently - many species once called 'Coprinus' are now in different genera, though Shaggy Manes kept their original scientific name.
compareHints: While there are no other true Coprinus species in our dataset for New England, Shaggy Manes are easily distinguished from other inky cap mushrooms by their large size, distinctive shaggy white scales, and cylindrical shape when young. Other small dark ink caps lack the prominent white scales and start out much smaller and grayer.
